title: Ἡ τῶν πτωχῶν μάχη
about: Irus, the town's public beggar, comes to the hall and orders the stranger off the threshold; Odysseus, in his rags, answers him calmly and warns him, and Irus loses his temper. Antinous, amused, proposes that the two settle it by fighting, with a roasted goat's paunch as the prize and a permanent place at the table for the winner. Odysseus, playing the weak old man, makes the suitors swear not to interfere, and Telemachus, as host, backs him. When Odysseus girds himself and shows his thighs and shoulders, with Athena enlarging his limbs, the suitors are astonished and Irus is forced into the ring trembling with fear, Antinous threatening him with mutilation if he loses. Odysseus weighs killing him against sparing him and chooses a measured blow that crushes the bones beneath Irus's ear; he drags Irus out to the courtyard and sets him against the wall with a staff and a warning.

sentences.t:
ἦλθε δ’ ἐπὶ πτωχὸς πανδήμιος, ὃς κατὰ ἄστυ
πτωχεύεσκ’ Ἰθάκης, μετὰ δ’ ἔπρεπε γαστέρι μάργῃ
ἀζηχὲς φαγέμεν καὶ πιέμεν·
sentences.i: Then a public beggar appeared, one who used to beg all over the town of Ithaca and stood out among them for a ravenous belly that kept him eating and drinking without end;
sentences.n: ἦλθε … ἐπί is a verb with its preverb standing apart (Attic ἐπῆλθε), ‘came on the scene’. πανδήμιος ‘of all the people’ makes him the town’s common beggar, one who asked of everyone. πτωχεύεσκ’ is an iterative imperfect in -σκ-, ‘used to beg’, a form Homer uses for habit. Ἰθάκης is the genitive of Ἰθάκη, ‘of Ithaca’, depending on ἄστυ. μάργῃ is ‘raging, frenzied’ (the dictionaries also give ‘greedy’); here it describes the belly, and the dative γαστέρι says what he stood out for. ἀζηχές ‘unceasingly’ is adverbial, and φαγέμεν and πιέμεν are infinitives in -έμεν (Attic φαγεῖν, πιεῖν).

sentences.t:
οὐδέ οἱ ἦν ἲς
οὐδὲ βίη, εἶδος δὲ μάλα μέγας ἦν ὁράασθαι.
sentences.l:
nor to him was there force
nor might, but in form very great he was to look at.
sentences.i: and he had neither force nor might, though in build he was very big to look at.
sentences.n: οὐδέ οἱ ἦν is ‘and there was not to him’, the dative οἱ ‘to him’ with ἦν ‘was’ as the Greek way of saying ‘he had’. ἲς ‘force’ and βίη ‘might’ name the strength he lacks, and the second clause sets his bulk against it. εἶδος is an accusative of respect, ‘in form, as to build’, and ὁράασθαι is the infinitive of ὁράομαι with the vowel stretched (Attic ὁρᾶσθαι), ‘to be looked at’.

sentences.t: Ἀρναῖος δ’ ὄνομ’ ἔσκε·
sentences.l: And Arnaeus was his name;
sentences.i: His name was Arnaeus;
sentences.n: Ἀρναῖος is the name his mother gave him; its meaning is not known, though it looks like a relative of ἀρήν, ἀρνός ‘lamb’, and that is only a guess. ἔσκε is an epic past of εἰμί in -σκ-, ‘was’; the nickname Ἶρος follows at 6.

sentences.t:
τὸ γὰρ θέτο πότνια μήτηρ
ἐκ γενετῆς·
sentences.l:
for that she gave, the lady mother,
from birth;
sentences.i: for his lady mother had given him that name from birth;
sentences.n: τὸ ‘that’ points back to ὄνομα, the name. θέτο is the unaugmented aorist middle of τίθημι ‘put, give’; the middle voice says the mother gave the name to her own child. πότνια ‘lady’ is the respectful title used of goddesses and of the mistress of a house, here of the mother. γενετῆς is the genitive of γενετή ‘birth’, governed by ἐκ.

sentences.t:
Ἶρον δὲ νέοι κίκλησκον ἅπαντες,
οὕνεκ’ ἀπαγγέλλεσκε κιών, ὅτε πού τις ἀνώγοι·
sentences.l:
but Irus all the young men used to call him,
because he would carry word, going, whenever anyone might bid him;
sentences.i: but all the young men used to call him Irus, because he would go and carry messages whenever anyone told him to;
sentences.n: Ἶρον is the nickname, and the line says where it comes from: ἀπαγγέλλεσκε is an iterative in -σκ- ‘used to carry word’, and κίκλησκον is the imperfect of κικλήσκω, the reduplicated present of καλέω (Attic ἐκάλουν), ‘used to call’; the -σκ- there belongs to the present stem and is not the iterative suffix. The name echoes Ἶρις, the gods’ messenger, though the line says only that he ran errands. νέοι is ‘young men’ used as a noun. οὕνεκ’ is οὕνεκα ‘because’. ὅτε πού τις ἀνώγοι is a general condition with the optative, ‘whenever anyone might bid him’.

sentences.t:
ὅς ῥ’ ἐλθὼν Ὀδυσῆα διώκετο οἷο δόμοιο,
καί μιν νεικείων ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
who, having come, was chasing Odysseus from his own house,
and, reviling him, winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: He came and set about driving Odysseus out of his own house, and, reviling him, spoke winged words:
sentences.n: ὅς ‘who’ continues the description of Irus. διώκετο is an imperfect that shows the attempt, ‘was chasing’, with οἷο δόμοιο ‘from his house’, a genitive of separation; οἷο is the epic possessive ‘his own’ and is taken here to refer to Odysseus, so that Irus tries to drive the man out of his own house. νεικείων is the participle of νεικείω ‘reproach, revile’. ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα is the stock introduction ‘spoke winged words’.

sentences.t: εἶκε, γέρον, προθύρου, μὴ δὴ τάχα καὶ ποδὸς ἕλκῃ.
sentences.l: “Give way, old man, from the forecourt, lest soon even by the foot you be dragged.
sentences.i: “Give way, old man, away from the forecourt, or soon you will be dragged out even by the foot.
sentences.n: Irus speaks, and his first word is the imperative εἶκε ‘yield’. προθύρου is a genitive of separation, ‘away from the forecourt’, the space before the doors where the beggar sits. μὴ δὴ τάχα … ἕλκῃ is a clause of fear, ‘lest soon’. The form ἕλκῃ can be read as a second-person passive, ‘you be dragged’, which is how l takes it, or as ‘someone drag you’, since the next line has the suitors urging him to drag the stranger; either way καὶ ποδός ‘even by the foot’ is the threat, and it comes back at 101.

sentences.t:
οὐκ ἀΐεις ὅτι δή μοι ἐπιλλίζουσιν ἅπαντες,
ἑλκέμεναι δὲ κέλονται;
sentences.l:
Do you not notice that they all are winking at me,
and are bidding me to drag you?
sentences.i: Don’t you notice that they are all winking at me and urging me to drag you out?
sentences.n: ἀΐεις (ἀΐω) is ‘perceive, notice’, addressed to Odysseus. ἐπιλλίζουσιν ‘wink at’ describes the suitors’ nods of encouragement to Irus. ἑλκέμεναι is an infinitive in -έμεναι (Attic ἕλκειν), and the object ‘you’ is left to be understood. The question ends in the middle of line 12 at the Greek question mark ;.

sentences.t: ἐγὼ δ’ αἰσχύνομαι ἔμπης.
sentences.l: Yet I am ashamed all the same.
sentences.i: Yet I am ashamed, all the same.
sentences.n: ἔμπης is ‘all the same, nevertheless’. It sets Irus’s shame against the suitors’ urging and makes him the reluctant party, who is only giving fair warning. αἰσχύνομαι is ‘I feel shame’.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄνα, μὴ τάχα νῶϊν ἔρις καὶ χερσὶ γένηται.
sentences.l: But up, lest soon between us two strife even with hands arise.”
sentences.i: So get up, or strife may soon break out between the two of us, even with fists.”
sentences.n: ἄνα is the preposition ἀνά standing alone as an imperative, ‘up!’, short for ‘stand up’. νῶϊν is the dual dative of ἐγώ, ‘for us two’; the dual is used when exactly two persons are meant, and returns in ἐρίζετον (38) and τὼ … ἄμφω (89). ἔρις καὶ χερσί ‘strife even with hands’ means that it will come to blows; γένηται is a subjunctive after μὴ τάχα.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπόδρα ἰδὼν προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.l: Him then with a scowl looking addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: Then Odysseus of many wiles, looking at him with a scowl, spoke to him:
sentences.n: A speech-introduction that comes round again: ὑπόδρα ἰδών is ‘looking from under (the brows)’, a dark, threatening look, which the house rendering gives as ‘with a scowl’. προσέφη is the aorist of πρόσφημι ‘speak to, address’. πολύμητις is the stock epithet of Odysseus, ‘of many wiles’ (μῆτις ‘cunning, craft’), translated each time it occurs.

sentences.t:
δαιμόνι’, οὔτε τί σε ῥέζω κακὸν οὔτ’ ἀγορεύω,
οὔτε τινὰ φθονέω δόμεναι καὶ πόλλ’ ἀνελόντα.
sentences.l:
“Strange man, neither do I do you any evil nor speak it,
nor do I begrudge that anyone give, even taking up much.
sentences.i: “Strange man, I do you no harm and say nothing against you, and I do not begrudge anyone for giving, even if he takes up a great deal to give.
sentences.n: δαιμόνιε (here elided) is an address whose force is uncertain, ‘strange one’, perhaps ‘one driven by something beyond himself’; here it chides. ῥέζω and ἀγορεύω both have κακόν as their object, ‘do or say any harm’. φθονέω ‘begrudge’ takes the infinitive δόμεναι (aorist infinitive of δίδωμι in -μεναι). The participle ἀνελόντα, from ἀναιρέω ‘take up’, agrees with τινά; it is understood as the giver lifting a great deal from the store to give away, and that is a reading of a compressed phrase rather than a certainty.

sentences.t:
οὐδὸς δ’ ἀμφοτέρους ὅδε χείσεται, οὐδέ τί σε χρὴ
ἀλλοτρίων φθονέειν·
sentences.l:
This threshold will hold us both, and there is no need for you
to begrudge what belongs to others;
sentences.i: This threshold will take us both, and you have no need to begrudge what belongs to others;
sentences.n: χείσεται is the future of χανδάνω ‘hold, have room for’: the threshold has room for two. οὐδέ τί σε χρή is ‘and there is no need for you’. φθονέειν is the uncontracted infinitive (Attic φθονεῖν), and it takes the genitive ἀλλοτρίων ‘of what belongs to others’. The verb is the same one that Odysseus used of himself in the line before, φθονέω ‘I begrudge’.

sentences.t:
δοκέεις δέ μοι εἶναι ἀλήτης
ὥς περ ἐγών, ὄλβον δὲ θεοὶ μέλλουσιν ὀπάζειν.
sentences.l:
You seem to me to be a vagrant
just as I am, and prosperity the gods are likely to bestow.
sentences.i: You seem to me to be a vagrant just as I am, and prosperity is what the gods are likely to grant.
sentences.n: δοκέεις … εἶναι is ‘you seem to be’, with δοκέεις uncontracted. ἀλήτης ‘vagrant’ is the poem’s word for a wanderer without a home, which Odysseus applies to both of them. ὥς περ ἐγών is ‘just as I (am)’. μέλλουσιν ὀπάζειν is ‘are likely to bestow, are about to grant’; ὄλβος ‘prosperity’ is the blessed state of having enough. The line does not say to which of the two the gods will give it.

sentences.t:
χερσὶ δὲ μή τι λίην προκαλίζεο, μή με χολώσῃς,
μή σε γέρων περ ἐὼν στῆθος καὶ χείλεα φύρσω
αἵματος·
sentences.i: But do not challenge me too much with your fists, and do not anger me, or old as I am I will smear your chest and lips with blood;
sentences.n: προκαλίζεο is the present imperative of προκαλίζομαι ‘challenge’ (to a fight), with χερσί ‘with the hands’. μή με χολώσῃς is a prohibition with the aorist subjunctive, ‘do not anger me’. μή σε … φύρσω is a clause of fear used as a threat, ‘lest I smear you’, with φύρσω an aorist subjunctive of φύρω ‘mix, smear’. σε and στῆθος καὶ χείλεα are the whole and the part: ‘you, as to chest and lips’. γέρων περ ἐὼν is ‘old though I am’, περ giving the participle concessive force. αἵματος is a genitive ‘with blood’.

sentences.t:
ἡσυχίη δ’ ἂν ἐμοὶ καὶ μᾶλλον ἔτ’ εἴη
αὔριον·
sentences.l:
and quiet for me even more yet would be
tomorrow;
sentences.i: and I should have still more peace tomorrow;
sentences.n: ἡσυχίη is ‘quiet, peace’. ἂν … εἴη is the optative of what would be: the point is that a beaten Irus will no longer trouble him. καὶ μᾶλλον ἔτ’ is ‘even more still’, and αὔριον ‘tomorrow’ opens line 23 and, standing there at the raised dot, ends the unit.

sentences.t:
οὐ μὲν γάρ τί σ’ ὑποστρέψεσθαι ὀΐω
δεύτερον ἐς μέγαρον Λαερτιάδεω Ὀδυσῆος.
sentences.l:
for in no way do I think you will return
a second time to the hall of Laertes’ son Odysseus.”
sentences.i: for I do not think you will come back to the hall of Odysseus, son of Laertes, a second time.”
sentences.n: ὑποστρέψεσθαι is the future infinitive of ὑποστρέφω ‘turn back, return’ in the middle, depending on ὀΐω ‘I think’. Λαερτιάδεω is the genitive of Λαερτιάδης ‘son of Laertes’ in -εω, and Ὀδυσῆος is the genitive Ὀδυσσῆος with one σ. Odysseus here names himself, in the third person, as the owner of the hall, to a man who does not know him.

sentences.t: τὸν δὲ χολωσάμενος προσεφώνεεν Ἶρος ἀλήτης·
sentences.l: And him, enraged, addressed Irus the vagrant:
sentences.i: Then Irus the vagrant, enraged, spoke to him:
sentences.n: χολωσάμενος ‘having become angry’ is the aorist middle participle of χολόω, the verb Odysseus used at 20, μή με χολώσῃς ‘do not anger me’. προσεφώνεεν is the uncontracted imperfect of προσφωνέω ‘address’. Ἶρος ἀλήτης, name and ‘vagrant’, is kept the same each time. The line has no ‘answered’, because the verb of speaking is προσεφώνεεν.

sentences.t:
ὢ πόποι, ὡς ὁ μολοβρὸς ἐπιτροχάδην ἀγορεύει,
γρηῒ καμινοῖ ἶσος·
sentences.l:
“Ah, how the scrounger glibly speaks,
like an old furnace-woman;
sentences.i: “Ah, how glibly the scrounger talks, just like an old furnace-woman;
sentences.n: ὢ πόποι is an exclamation of surprise or indignation, here ‘Ah,’. μολοβρός is a word whose meaning is not known; ‘glutton’ and ‘scrounger’ are ancient guesses, and ‘scrounger’ is used here. ἐπιτροχάδην ‘glibly’ is from τρέχω ‘run’, words that run on. γρηῒ is the dative of γρηῦς ‘old woman’ (Attic γραῦς), and with ἶσος ‘equal to’ it takes the dative. καμινοῖ is the dative of a rare noun, taken here as ‘furnace-woman’, a woman who tends the oven; the insult compares him to an old woman.

sentences.t:
ὃν ἂν κακὰ μητισαίμην
κόπτων ἀμφοτέρῃσι, χαμαὶ δέ κε πάντας ὀδόντας
γναθμῶν ἐξελάσαιμι συὸς ὣς ληϊβοτείρης.
sentences.l:
whom I would devise evils against,
striking with both, and on the ground all his teeth
from his jaws I would drive out, like a crop-ravaging sow’s.
sentences.i: I would devise harm for that man, striking him with both fists, and knock all his teeth out of his jaws onto the ground, like the teeth of a sow that ravages the crops.
sentences.n: ὃν is masculine and refers back to the μολοβρός, though the comparison was to a woman. ὃν ἂν … μητισαίμην is a relative clause with the optative, ‘whom I would plot against’, with κακά ‘evils’ as object. ἀμφοτέρῃσι is feminine, ‘with both (hands)’, χερσί being understood. ἐξελάσαιμι is the aorist optative of ἐξελαύνω ‘drive out’. συὸς ὣς ληϊβοτείρης is ‘like a crop-ravaging sow’s’, the genitive συός standing for the sow’s teeth, so that the comparison is with the teeth and not with the man: συός is the genitive of σῦς, ληϊβοτείρης is the feminine, from λήϊον ‘standing grain’ and the root of βόσκω ‘feed’.

sentences.t:
ζῶσαι νῦν, ἵνα πάντες ἐπιγνώωσι καὶ οἵδε
μαρναμένους·
sentences.l:
Gird yourself now, so that all, these here too, may take note
of us fighting;
sentences.i: Gird yourself now, so that everyone, these men here too, may see us fighting;
sentences.n: ζῶσαι is the aorist middle imperative of ζώννυμι ‘gird’: the beggar must tie up his rags before a fight, as Odysseus does at 67. ἐπιγνώωσι is an aorist subjunctive of ἐπιγιγνώσκω ‘take note of, recognise’ with the vowel stretched (Attic ἐπιγνῶσι). οἵδε ‘these here’ points at the suitors standing round. μαρναμένους is accusative plural, the unspoken ‘us’ fighting.

sentences.t: πῶς δ’ ἂν σὺ νεωτέρῳ ἀνδρὶ μάχοιο;
sentences.l: but how could you fight with a younger man?”
sentences.i: How could you possibly fight a younger man?”
sentences.n: πῶς … ἂν … μάχοιο is the optative of what could be, in a question: ‘how could you fight?’, and it is scornful, since Irus believes the old man cannot. μάχομαι takes the dative νεωτέρῳ ἀνδρί ‘with a younger man’; νεωτέρῳ is the comparative of νέος, ‘younger (than you)’.

sentences.t:
ὣς οἱ μὲν προπάροιθε θυράων ὑψηλάων
οὐδοῦ ἔπι ξεστοῦ πανθυμαδὸν ὀκριόωντο.
sentences.l:
So they, in front of the doors, the lofty ones,
on the threshold, the polished one, with all their heart were working each other up.
sentences.i: So the two of them, in front of the lofty doors, on the polished threshold, were working each other up with all their heart.
sentences.n: ὣς οἱ μέν ‘so they’ looks forward to the δέ at 34, which brings in Antinous. οἱ is the pronoun ‘they’, the two beggars. θυράων and ὑψηλάων are genitives plural in -άων (Attic θυρῶν, ὑψηλῶν). οὐδοῦ ἔπι is ‘on the threshold’, with ἔπι placed after its noun, and ξεστοῦ means smoothed. πανθυμαδόν ‘with all one’s heart’ is an adverb. ὀκριόωντο is a rare verb, with the vowels stretched (Attic ὀκριῶντο); ‘work each other up’ is the sense taken from the context.

sentences.t:
τοῖϊν δὲ ξυνέηχ’ ἱερὸν μένος Ἀντινόοιο,
ἡδὺ δ’ ἄρ’ ἐκγελάσας μετεφώνει μνηστήρεσσιν·
sentences.l:
And to the two gave ear the sacred strength of Antinous,
and sweetly, then, laughing out, he spoke among the suitors:
sentences.i: The sacred strength of Antinous heard the two of them, and with a pleasant laugh he spoke among the suitors:
sentences.n: ἱερὸν μένος Ἀντινόοιο is a periphrasis for Antinous, ‘the sacred strength of Antinous’, built like ἱερὴ ἲς Τηλεμάχοιο at 60; it replaces the bare name and is not turned into ‘mighty Antinous’. Ἀντινόοιο is a genitive in -οιο. ξυνέηχ’ is ξυνέηκε, the aorist of συνίημι ‘hear, take in’, here with the dual τοῖϊν, ‘the two’ (one form serves as genitive and dative). ἡδύ ‘sweetly’ is an adverb with ἐκγελάσας ‘laughing out’. μετεφώνει is ‘spoke among’, and the dative μνηστήρεσσιν is in -εσσι.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλοι, οὐ μέν πώ τι πάρος τοιοῦτον ἐτύχθη,
οἵην τερπωλὴν θεὸς ἤγαγεν ἐς τόδε δῶμα.
sentences.l:
“O friends, not yet before has anything of such a kind come about,
such delight as a god has brought to this house.
sentences.i: “Friends, nothing like this has ever happened before, such a delight as a god has brought into this house.
sentences.n: ὦ φίλοι ‘O friends’ is a speaker’s address to his own company. ἐτύχθη is the aorist passive of τεύχω ‘make’, ‘came to be, came about’. οἵην picks up τοιοῦτον: ‘of such a kind, such as’, and τερπωλή is ‘delight, amusement’. The ‘delight’ is the fight, and the ‘god’ is left unnamed.

sentences.t:
ὁ ξεῖνός τε καὶ Ἶρος ἐρίζετον ἀλλήλοιϊν
χερσὶ μαχέσσασθαι·
sentences.l:
The stranger and Irus are rivalling one another
to fight with their hands;
sentences.i: The stranger and Irus are rivalling each other in a fist fight;
sentences.n: ὁ ξεῖνος ‘the stranger’ is Antinous’s name for Odysseus. ἐρίζετον is the third person dual of ἐρίζω ‘rival, strive’, since there are two contestants, and ἀλλήλοιϊν is the dual dative ‘with each other’. μαχέσσασθαι is the aorist infinitive of μάχομαι with doubled σ (Attic μαχέσασθαι), and χερσί ‘with the hands’ is the fist-fight.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ ξυνελάσσομεν ὦκα.
sentences.l: but let us set them together quickly.”
sentences.i: Come, let us quickly bring them to blows.”
sentences.n: ξυνελάσσομεν is an aorist subjunctive with the short vowel (Attic συνελάσωμεν), used as an exhortation, ‘let us’. συνελαύνω ‘drive together’ is said of setting two fighters at each other. ὦκα ‘quickly’ is an adverb.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἱ δ’ ἄρα πάντες ἀνήϊξαν γελόωντες,
ἀμφὶ δ’ ἄρα πτωχοὺς κακοείμονας ἠγερέθοντο.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and they then, all of them, leapt up laughing,
and around the beggars, the ill-clad ones, they gathered.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they all sprang up laughing and crowded round the two ragged beggars.
sentences.n: ἔφαθ’ is ἔφατο with the vowel dropped. ἀνήϊξαν is the aorist of ἀναΐσσω ‘spring up’. γελόωντες is the open form of γελῶντες ‘laughing’, with diectasis. ἀμφὶ … ἠγερέθοντο is the preverb standing apart from its verb, ‘gathered round’, ἠγερέθοντο being a longer form of the middle of ἀγείρω. κακοείμονας ‘ill-clad’ is κακός ‘bad’ with εἷμα ‘garment’; the two beggars are meant.

sentences.t: τοῖσιν δ’ Ἀντίνοος μετέφη, Εὐπείθεος υἱός·
sentences.l: Among them then spoke Antinous, Eupeithes’ son:
sentences.i: Among them Antinous, son of Eupeithes, spoke:
sentences.n: μετέφη is ‘spoke among’, the speaker addressing the whole company. The patronymic Εὐπείθεος υἱός ‘son of Eupeithes’ has a genitive in -εος (Attic -ους).

sentences.t: κέκλυτέ μευ, μνηστῆρες ἀγήνορες, ὄφρα τι εἴπω.
sentences.l: “Hear me, lordly suitors, so that I may say something.
sentences.i: “Hear me, lordly suitors, so that I may say something.
sentences.n: κέκλυτε is the reduplicated aorist imperative of κλύω ‘hear’, and μευ is the genitive of ἐγώ (Attic μου), ‘hear me’. μνηστῆρες ἀγήνορες is the stock address and is rendered ‘lordly suitors’ each time. ὄφρα ‘so that’ takes the aorist subjunctive εἴπω.

sentences.t:
γαστέρες αἵδ’ αἰγῶν κέατ’ ἐν πυρί, τὰς ἐπὶ δόρπῳ
κατθέμεθα κνίσης τε καὶ αἵματος ἐμπλήσαντες·
sentences.l:
These bellies of goats lie in the fire, which for supper
we set down, having filled them with fat and blood;
sentences.i: These goats’ paunches are lying in the fire, which we put there for our supper after stuffing them with fat and blood;
sentences.n: γαστέρες … αἰγῶν are the stomachs of goats, stuffed and roasted like a sausage; the next line says with what. αἵδε is ‘these here’, and κέατ’ is κέαται, the third person plural of κεῖμαι ‘lie’. κατθέμεθα is the aorist middle of κατατίθημι ‘set down’, with κατ- standing for κατά with its last vowel cut off. κνίσης is usually the smell of cooking fat; for something put inside a paunch it can only be the fat itself, and ‘fat’ is used. ἐμπλήσαντες is the aorist participle of ἐμπίμπλημι ‘fill’, taking the genitives κνίσης and αἵματος.

sentences.t:
ὁππότερος δέ κε νικήσῃ κρείσσων τε γένηται,
τάων ἥν κ’ ἐθέλῃσιν ἀναστὰς αὐτὸς ἑλέσθω·
sentences.l:
and whichever of the two wins and proves the stronger,
of these whichever he wishes, rising, himself let him choose;
sentences.i: and whichever of the two wins and proves the stronger, let him stand up and himself take whichever of them he likes;
sentences.n: ὁππότερος is ‘whichever of the two’ (Attic ὁπότερος). κε and κ’ are the particle ἄν with the subjunctive in a general condition, ‘whoever wins’. κρείσσων is the comparative ‘stronger’. τάων is the epic genitive plural of the feminine pronoun, ‘of these (bellies)’. ἑλέσθω is the aorist middle imperative of αἱρέω, ‘let him take for himself’.

sentences.t:
αἰεὶ αὖθ’ ἡμῖν μεταδαίσεται, οὐδέ τιν’ ἄλλον
πτωχὸν ἔσω μίσγεσθαι ἐάσομεν αἰτήσοντα.
sentences.l:
and always hereafter among us he shall feast, and no other
beggar to mingle inside shall we allow, in order to beg.”
sentences.i: and he will feast among us always from now on, and we will let no other beggar in to mix with us and beg.”
sentences.n: αὖθ’ could be αὖθι ‘on the spot’ or αὖτε ‘again’; with αἰεί the sense taken is ‘always hereafter’. μεταδαίσεται is a future of μεταδαίνυμαι ‘feast among’, with μετα- ‘among’ as in μετέφη. οὐδέ τιν’ ἄλλον πτωχόν … ἐάσομεν is ‘and we shall allow no other beggar’, with the infinitive μίσγεσθαι ‘to mix (with us)’ and ἔσω ‘inside’. αἰτήσοντα is a future participle expressing purpose, ‘in order to ask (for food)’.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’ Ἀντίνοος, τοῖσιν δ’ ἐπιήνδανε μῦθος.
sentences.l: So spoke Antinous, and to them the word was pleasing.
sentences.i: So spoke Antinous, and his words pleased them.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ Ἀντίνοος is the speech-closing formula with the speaker’s name filled in, ‘So spoke Antinous’. ἐπιήνδανε is the imperfect of ἐπιανδάνω ‘please, be pleasing to’, which takes the dative τοῖσιν ‘to them’; the augment and the first vowel of the stem have run together in -ήν-. μῦθος is a ‘speech, word, proposal’.

sentences.t: τοῖς δὲ δολοφρονέων μετέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.l: And among them, with guile in his mind, spoke many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: Among them Odysseus of many wiles, with guile in his mind, spoke:
sentences.n: δολοφρονέων ‘with a crafty mind’ is δόλος ‘guile’ with φρήν ‘mind’; the speech that follows plays the part of a feeble old man, and the epithet tells the hearer so in advance. μετέφη ‘spoke among’ and πολύμητις ‘of many wiles’ keep their house renderings.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλοι, οὔ πως ἔστι νεωτέρῳ ἀνδρὶ μάχεσθαι
ἄνδρα γέροντα, δύῃ ἀρημένον·
sentences.l:
“O friends, in no way is it possible with a younger man to fight,
an old man, afflicted with distress;
sentences.i: “Friends, there is no way for an old man, worn down by distress, to fight a younger man;
sentences.n: οὔ πως ἔστι is ‘it is in no way possible’. νεωτέρῳ ἀνδρί is the dative with μάχεσθαι, and ἄνδρα γέροντα is the accusative subject of the infinitive, ‘for an old man to fight’. ἀρημένον ‘afflicted, worn down’ is a participle-adjective whose origin is uncertain, and δύῃ ‘distress, misery’ gives the cause. Antinous will repeat the words ἄνδρα γέροντα, δύῃ ἀρημένον at 81.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά με γαστὴρ
ὀτρύνει κακοεργός, ἵνα πληγῇσι δαμείω.
sentences.l:
but me the belly
urges on, the evil-working one, so that by blows I be subdued.
sentences.i: but my belly, which works me harm, drives me on, so that I will be beaten down by blows.
sentences.n: γαστήρ ‘belly’ stands for his hunger, as in the description of Irus at 2. κακοεργός ‘evil-working’ is κακός with ἔργον. ὀτρύνει is ‘urges on’. δαμείω is the aorist passive subjunctive of δάμνημι ‘subdue’ with the Homeric ending -είω (Attic δαμῶ), and πληγῇσι is the dative plural in -ῃσι, ‘by blows’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε νῦν μοι πάντες ὀμόσσατε καρτερὸν ὅρκον,
μή τις ἐπ’ Ἴρῳ ἦρα φέρων ἐμὲ χειρὶ βαρείῃ
πλήξῃ ἀτασθάλλων, τούτῳ δέ με ἶφι δαμάσσῃ.
sentences.l:
But come now, to me all swear a mighty oath,
that no one, for Irus bringing favour, me with a heavy hand
strike, acting wantonly, and to this man’s advantage by force subdue me.”
sentences.i: But come now, all of you swear me a solemn oath, that no one will strike me with a heavy hand, in wanton favour to Irus, and overpower me by force to this man’s advantage.”
sentences.n: ὀμόσσατε is the aorist imperative of ὄμνυμι with doubled σ (Attic ὀμόσατε); ὅρκον ‘oath’ is the thing sworn, and καρτερός ‘mighty’ is the oath’s strength. μή τις … πλήξῃ … δαμάσσῃ is a μή clause with the subjunctive giving the content of the oath, ‘that no one …’. ἦρα φέρων ‘bringing a favour’ means doing a service to someone, here ἐπ’ Ἴρῳ ‘for Irus’. ἀτασθάλλων is ‘acting wantonly, recklessly’, the verb of ἀτασθαλίη. ἶφι is ‘by force’, and χειρὶ βαρείῃ ‘with a heavy hand’ is a dative of means.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἱ δ’ ἄρα πάντες ἀπώμνυον ὡς ἐκέλευεν.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and they then, all of them, swore as he bade.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they all swore as he told them to.
sentences.n: ἀπώμνυον is the imperfect of ἀπόμνυμι, which is ‘swear not to’, an oath of refusal; the oath here is not to help Irus. The imperfect shows them swearing one after another, and ὡς ἐκέλευεν ‘as he bade’ shows that they took the oath in the words he had given.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ῥ’ ὄμοσάν τε τελεύτησάν τε τὸν ὅρκον,
τοῖς δ’ αὖτις μετέειφ’ ἱερὴ ἲς Τηλεμάχοιο·
sentences.l:
But when then they had sworn and completed the oath,
then among them again spoke the sacred force of Telemachus:
sentences.i: When they had sworn and completed the oath, the strong, sacred figure of Telemachus spoke among them again:
sentences.n: ὄμοσάν τε τελεύτησάν τε is ‘they swore and they completed’, two aorists coupled by τε … τε; τελευτάω is ‘bring to an end’. μετέειφ’ is μετέειπε, ‘spoke among’, with the final vowel dropped and the π made φ before the rough breathing of ἱερή. ἱερὴ ἲς Τηλεμάχοιο is a periphrasis for Telemachus, ‘the sacred force of Telemachus’, kept in l and i in place of a bare name, like ἱερὸν μένος Ἀντινόοιο at 34.

sentences.t:
ξεῖν’, εἴ σ’ ὀτρύνει κραδίη καὶ θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ
τοῦτον ἀλέξασθαι, τῶν δ’ ἄλλων μή τιν’ Ἀχαιῶν
δείδιθ’, ἐπεὶ πλεόνεσσι μαχήσεται ὅς κέ σε θείνῃ·
sentences.i: “Stranger, if your heart and proud spirit urge you to defend yourself against this man, do not fear any of the other Achaeans, since whoever strikes you will have to fight more men;
sentences.n: ξεῖν’ ‘stranger’ is the polite address, here from the host. κραδίη καὶ θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ is ‘heart and manly spirit’; the verb ὀτρύνει is singular though it has two subjects. ἀλέξασθαι is the aorist infinitive middle of ἀλέξω, ‘ward off, defend oneself against’. δείδιθ’ is the perfect imperative of δείδω ‘fear’. πλεόνεσσι is a dative in -εσσι, ‘with more’. ὅς κέ σε θείνῃ is a general relative clause, ‘whoever strikes you’.

sentences.t:
ξεινοδόκος μὲν ἐγών, ἐπὶ δ’ αἰνεῖτον βασιλῆες,
Ἀντίνοός τε καὶ Εὐρύμαχος, πεπνυμένω ἄμφω.
sentences.l:
I am one who receives guests, and besides the two kings approve,
Antinous and Eurymachus, prudent both.”
sentences.i: I am your host, and the two kings, Antinous and Eurymachus, both prudent men, approve.”
sentences.n: ξεινοδόκος is ‘one who receives a guest’, ξεῖνος with δέχομαι. ἐπὶ … αἰνεῖτον is the preverb separated from its verb, ἐπαινέω ‘approve’, and the verb is dual, since two kings are named. Ἀντίνοός τε καὶ Εὐρύμαχος stands in apposition to βασιλῆες. πεπνυμένω is the dual of the perfect participle πεπνυμένος ‘prudent’, and ἄμφω ‘both’ is dual too.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἱ δ’ ἄρα πάντες ἐπῄνεον·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and they then all praised it;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they all applauded;
sentences.n: ἐπῄνεον is the uncontracted imperfect of ἐπαινέω ‘praise, applaud’, the same verb Telemachus used of the two kings at 64, there in two parts and in the sense ‘approve’. ἔφαθ’ is ἔφατο with the vowel dropped.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ὀδυσσεὺς
ζώσατο μὲν ῥάκεσιν περὶ μήδεα, φαῖνε δὲ μηροὺς
καλούς τε μεγάλους τε, φάνεν δέ οἱ εὐρέες ὦμοι
στήθεά τε στιβαροί τε βραχίονες·
sentences.l:
but Odysseus
girded himself with rags around his genitals, and showed his thighs,
fair and great, and there appeared his broad shoulders,
and chests, and stout arms;
sentences.i: but Odysseus girded himself with rags about his genitals and showed his thighs, fair and great, and his broad shoulders came into view, with his chest and his stout arms;
sentences.n: ζώσατο is the aorist middle of ζώννυμι ‘gird’, as Irus was told to do at 30; ῥάκεσιν ‘with rags’ is a dative. μήδεα here means the genitals, a different word from μήδεα ‘counsels’, and is not softened. The μέν and δέ set the girding beside the showing. μηροὺς καλούς τε μεγάλους τε is ‘thighs both fair and great’. φάνεν is the aorist passive (Attic ἐφάνησαν) ‘came into view’. εὐρέες is the uncontracted plural of εὐρύς ‘broad’, and στιβαροί is ‘stout’. ὦμοι, στήθεα and βραχίονες are the three subjects of φάνεν.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἀθήνη
ἄγχι παρισταμένη μέλε’ ἤλδανε ποιμένι λαῶν.
sentences.l:
but Athena,
close by, standing near, made grow the limbs of the shepherd of the people.
sentences.i: but Athena, standing close beside him, made the limbs of the shepherd of the people grow.
sentences.n: ἄγχι παρισταμένη is ‘standing close beside’, and Athena has not been named earlier in this part. ἤλδανε is the aorist of ἀλδαίνω ‘make grow, strengthen’, with μέλε’ (μέλεα with the vowel dropped) ‘limbs’ as its object. ποιμένι λαῶν ‘shepherd of the people’ is the stock title of a leader, here in the dative of interest, ‘for him’, which English gives as ‘the limbs of the shepherd’, and it is kept the same wherever it occurs.

sentences.t: μνηστῆρες δ’ ἄρα πάντες ὑπερφιάλως ἀγάσαντο·
sentences.l: And the suitors all then beyond measure were amazed;
sentences.i: And all the suitors were amazed beyond measure;
sentences.n: ὑπερφιάλως ‘beyond measure’ is the adverb of ὑπερφίαλος and is not the ‘overweening’ of the adjective. ἀγάσαντο is the aorist middle of ἀγάομαι ‘wonder at, marvel’. What the suitors said comes at 73–74, after the introduction at 72.

sentences.t: ὧδε δέ τις εἴπεσκεν ἰδὼν ἐς πλησίον ἄλλον·
sentences.l: And thus someone would say, looking to another close by:
sentences.i: And as each looked at the one beside him, he would say something like this:
sentences.n: ὧδε is ‘thus’ and looks forward to the speech. εἴπεσκεν is the iterative of εἶπον, ‘would say’: many of the suitors say it one after another, so the speech that follows is a chorus and not one man. ἐς πλησίον ἄλλον is ‘to another close by’.

sentences.t:
ἦ τάχα Ἶρος Ἄϊρος ἐπίσπαστον κακὸν ἕξει,
οἵην ἐκ ῥακέων ὁ γέρων ἐπιγουνίδα φαίνει.
sentences.l:
“Truly soon Irus, Un-Irus, an evil drawn on himself will have,
such a thigh out of his rags the old man shows.”
sentences.i: “Soon Irus, who will be Irus no more, will have an evil he has drawn down on himself, to judge by what a thigh the old man shows out of his rags.”
sentences.n: Ἶρος Ἄϊρος is a pun: the nickname with the negative prefix ἀ- gives ‘Un-Irus’, one who will be Irus no more; it is rendered with a hyphenated coinage in l. ἐπίσπαστον ‘drawn on’ (from ἐπισπάω) is an evil that one has pulled upon oneself. ἦ τάχα is ‘truly soon’. οἵην ἐπιγουνίδα is ‘what a thigh’, a relative-exclamatory οἷος giving the grounds of the prediction, and ἐπιγουνίς is the upper thigh. ὁ γέρων ‘the old man’ and ἐκ ῥακέων ‘out of the rags’, with ῥακέων the genitive plural in -έων, show the thigh that the girding left bare.

sentences.t: ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφαν, Ἴρῳ δὲ κακῶς ὠρίνετο θυμός.
sentences.l: So they spoke, and for Irus badly was stirred the heart.
sentences.i: So they spoke, and the heart of Irus was badly stirred.
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφαν is ‘so they spoke’, ἔφαν being the third person plural of ἔφην. Ἴρῳ is a dative of the person affected, ‘for Irus’. ὠρίνετο is the imperfect passive of ὀρίνω ‘stir up, shake’, and θυμός ‘heart’ is the seat of feeling.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ καὶ ὣς δρηστῆρες ἄγον ζώσαντες ἀνάγκῃ
δειδιότα·
sentences.l:
But even so the serving-men led him, having girded him, by force,
fearful;
sentences.i: But even so the serving-men girded him and led him out by force, quaking with fear;
sentences.n: ἀλλὰ καὶ ὣς is ‘but even so’, with ὥς the accented adverb. δρηστῆρες ‘serving-men’ are those who do the work, from δράω ‘do’. ζώσαντες is the aorist participle of ζώννυμι, ‘having girded (him)’: Irus had been told at 30 to gird himself, and now it is done for him. ἀνάγκῃ ‘by compulsion’ is a dative. δειδιότα is the perfect participle of δείδω ‘fear’, accusative, agreeing with the unspoken ‘him’.

sentences.t: σάρκες δὲ περιτρομέοντο μέλεσσιν.
sentences.l: and the flesh was trembling all round upon his limbs.
sentences.i: and the flesh quivered all over his limbs.
sentences.n: σάρκες is ‘flesh’ in the plural. περιτρομέοντο is the imperfect middle of περιτρομέω ‘tremble all round’, with the preverb περι-, uncontracted. μέλεσσιν is a dative plural in -εσσι, ‘on his limbs’.

sentences.t: Ἀντίνοος δ’ ἐνένιπεν ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζεν·
sentences.l: And Antinous rebuked him, and spoke a word, and called him by name:
sentences.i: Antinous rebuked him, and spoke, calling him by name:
sentences.n: ἐνένιπεν is the aorist of ἐνίπτω ‘rebuke, scold’, with Irus understood as the object. ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζεν is a stock formula for a speaker’s address, and ἔκ … ὀνόμαζεν is a verb with its preverb standing apart, ‘called by name’. It need not mean that a name is used: Antinous’s word for him in the next line is βουγάϊε, not Ἶρε.

sentences.t:
νῦν μὲν μήτ’ εἴης, βουγάϊε, μήτε γένοιο,
εἰ δὴ τοῦτόν γε τρομέεις καὶ δείδιας αἰνῶς,
ἄνδρα γέροντα, δύῃ ἀρημένον, ἥ μιν ἱκάνει.
sentences.i: “Would that you did not exist, braggart, and had never been born, if you really tremble at this man and are terribly afraid of him, an old man worn down by the distress that has come upon him.
sentences.n: μήτ’ εἴης … μήτε γένοιο is a wish in the optative, ‘may you neither be nor have been born’, a harsh curse. βουγάϊε (βουγάϊος) is an abusive word whose meaning is not known; ‘braggart’ is the usual guess, and its first part may be βοῦς ‘ox’. εἰ δὴ … γε is ‘if indeed’. τρομέεις is uncontracted, and δείδιας is the perfect of δείδω. ἄνδρα γέροντα, δύῃ ἀρημένον stands in apposition to τοῦτον and echoes Odysseus’s own words at 53. ἥ is the relative, ‘which’, referring to δύῃ, and μιν is ‘him’.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἔκ τοι ἐρέω, τὸ δὲ καὶ τετελεσμένον ἔσται·
sentences.l: But I will speak out plainly to you, and this too shall be a thing fulfilled;
sentences.i: But I will tell you plainly, and this too will come true:
sentences.n: ἔκ … ἐρέω is the verb with its preverb standing apart, ‘speak out, tell plainly’, and ἐρέω is a future. τοι is the dative ‘to you’. τετελεσμένον ἔσται, the perfect participle with ‘will be’, is ‘it will be a thing accomplished’.

sentences.t:
αἴ κέν σ’ οὗτος νικήσῃ κρείσσων τε γένηται,
πέμψω σ’ ἤπειρόνδε, βαλὼν ἐν νηὶ μελαίνῃ,
εἰς Ἔχετον βασιλῆα, βροτῶν δηλήμονα πάντων,
sentences.l:
If this man defeats you and proves the stronger,
I will send you to the mainland, throwing you into a black ship,
to Echetus the king, bane of all mortals,
sentences.i: If this man beats you and proves the stronger, I will throw you into a black ship and send you to the mainland, to King Echetus, the bane of all mortals,
sentences.n: αἴ κέν is αἰ and κε, ‘if’ with the aorist subjunctive. νικήσῃ κρείσσων τε γένηται repeats Antinous’s own wording from 46, where it was said of the prize. ἤπειρόνδε is ‘to the mainland’, the ending -δε marking direction. βαλὼν ἐν νηί is ‘having thrown (you) into a ship’, and νηὶ μελαίνῃ ‘black ship’ is the stock phrase. Ἔχετον βασιλῆα is a king of the mainland, and all this part says of him is his cruelty. δηλήμων ‘bane, one who does harm’ is the noun for one who damages.

sentences.t:
ὅς κ’ ἀπὸ ῥῖνα τάμῃσι καὶ οὔατα νηλέϊ χαλκῷ,
μήδεά τ’ ἐξερύσας δώῃ κυσὶν ὠμὰ δάσασθαι.
sentences.l:
who will cut off your nose and ears with pitiless bronze,
and, having torn out your genitals, give them to dogs, raw, to divide.”
sentences.i: who will cut off your nose and ears with pitiless bronze, and tear out your genitals and give them raw to the dogs to rend among themselves.”
sentences.n: ὅς κ’ … τάμῃσι is a relative with κε and the aorist subjunctive, ‘who will cut’, and ἀπὸ … τάμῃσι is the verb ἀποτάμνω with its preverb standing apart, ‘cut off’; σε is understood. ῥῖνα is ‘nose’, and οὔατα is the epic uncontracted form of ὦτα ‘ears’. νηλέϊ is ‘pitiless’, from ἔλεος ‘pity’ with the negative prefix. μήδεα is again ‘genitals’ (as at 67). ἐξερύσας is ‘having torn out’, and ὠμά ‘raw’ is an adjective in the neuter plural; δάσασθαι is the aorist infinitive middle of δατέομαι ‘divide among themselves’.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, τῷ δ’ ἔτι μᾶλλον ὑπὸ τρόμος ἔλλαβε γυῖα.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and him still more from beneath a trembling seized, the limbs.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and a trembling seized the limbs of Irus all the more.
sentences.n: τῷ ‘him’ is a dative of the person affected, and γυῖα ‘limbs’ is the accusative of the part seized. ὑπὸ … ἔλλαβε is the preverb standing apart from its verb, ‘seized from beneath’, said of a shudder that rises through the limbs. μᾶλλον ἔτι is ‘still more’.

sentences.t: ἐς μέσσον δ’ ἄναγον· τὼ δ’ ἄμφω χεῖρας ἀνέσχον.
sentences.l: Into the middle they led him up; and the two, both, their hands raised.
sentences.i: They led him out into the middle, and the two raised their hands.
sentences.n: ἄναγον is ‘led up’, the subject being the serving-men of 76, and ἐς μέσσον ‘into the middle’ is the open space made by the crowd. τὼ … ἄμφω is the dual, ‘the two of them both’. ἀνέσχον is the aorist of ἀνέχω ‘hold up’: they raise their fists to fight.

sentences.t:
δὴ τότε μερμήριξε πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεὺς
ἢ ἐλάσει’ ὥς μιν ψυχὴ λίποι αὖθι πεσόντα,
ἦέ μιν ἦκ’ ἐλάσειε τανύσσειέν τ’ ἐπὶ γαίῃ.
sentences.l:
Then indeed pondered much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus
whether he should strike so that him life would leave, right there, fallen,
or strike him lightly and stretch him out on the earth.
sentences.i: Then much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus wondered whether to strike him so that the life would leave him right there where he fell, or to strike him lightly and stretch him out on the ground.
sentences.n: μερμήριξε ‘pondered’ is the verb of a hero weighing two courses, and the two courses come as indirect questions, ἢ … ἦέ ‘whether … or’, with optatives. πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς is the name-formula, ‘much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus’. ἐλάσει’ is the optative ἐλάσειε of ἐλαύνω ‘drive, strike’. ὥς … λίποι is a clause with the optative, ‘so that life would leave him’, the purpose of the blow, and πεσόντα is the aorist participle, agreeing with μιν. ἦκ’ is ἦκα, ‘lightly, gently’. τανύσσειεν is the aorist optative of τανύω ‘stretch out’, with doubled σ.

sentences.t:
ὧδε δέ οἱ φρονέοντι δοάσσατο κέρδιον εἶναι,
ἦκ’ ἐλάσαι, ἵνα μή μιν ἐπιφρασσαίατ’ Ἀχαιοί.
sentences.l:
And thus to him considering it seemed better to be
to strike lightly, so that him they might not notice, the Achaeans.
sentences.i: And this, as he thought it over, seemed to him the better course: to strike lightly, so that the Achaeans would not notice him.
sentences.n: δοάσσατο is an epic aorist meaning ‘it seemed’, with the dative οἱ ‘to him’; κέρδιον ‘better, more profitable’ is the comparative of κέρδος ‘gain’. The infinitive ἐλάσαι ‘to strike’ says what seemed better. ἐπιφρασσαίατ’ is the aorist optative middle, third person plural, with the old ending -αίατο, ‘might notice’. Ἀχαιοί here are the men of the hall.

sentences.t:
δὴ τότ’ ἀνασχομένω ὁ μὲν ἤλασε δεξιὸν ὦμον
Ἶρος, ὁ δ’ αὐχέν’ ἔλασσεν ὑπ’ οὔατος, ὀστέα δ’ εἴσω
ἔθλασεν·
sentences.i: Then the two raised their fists, and Irus struck the right shoulder, but Odysseus struck the neck below the ear and crushed the bones inside;
sentences.n: ἀνασχομένω is a dual participle, ‘the two raising (their hands)’, as the dual τὼ … ἄμφω at 89. ὁ μὲν … Ἶρος, ὁ δ’ is ‘the one, Irus … the other’, with the name added after the pronoun. ἔλασσεν is the aorist of ἐλαύνω with doubled σ, the same ‘struck’ as ἤλασε. ὑπ’ οὔατος is ‘beneath the ear’, with οὔατος the epic genitive of οὖς. εἴσω is ‘within’. ἔθλασεν ‘crushed’ is from θλάω, and its subject is Odysseus.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκα δ’ ἦλθε κατὰ στόμα φοίνιον αἷμα,
κὰδ δ’ ἔπεσ’ ἐν κονίῃσι μακών, σὺν δ’ ἤλασ’ ὀδόντας
λακτίζων ποσὶ γαῖαν·
sentences.i: and at once red blood came out through his mouth, and he fell in the dust with a cry, gnashing his teeth and kicking the ground with his feet;
sentences.n: κατὰ στόμα is ‘down through the mouth’, and φοίνιον is ‘blood-red’. κὰδ is κατά with the final consonant changed before δ, ‘down’. ἐν κονίῃσι has the dative plural in -ῃσι, ‘in the dust’. μακών is the aorist participle of μηκάομαι, ‘cry out’, a verb used of the cries of animals. σὺν … ἤλασ’ ὀδόντας is the preverb standing apart, ‘drove his teeth together’, that is ‘gnashed’. λακτίζων ποσὶ γαῖαν is ‘kicking the ground with his feet’.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ μνηστῆρες ἀγαυοὶ
χεῖρας ἀνασχόμενοι γέλῳ ἔκθανον.
sentences.l:
but the noble suitors,
lifting up their hands, died with laughter.
sentences.i: while the noble suitors threw up their hands and died of laughter.
sentences.n: ἀτάρ is ‘but, and yet’. μνηστῆρες ἀγαυοί is ‘the noble suitors’; this is a separate epithet from ἀγήνορες ‘lordly’. χεῖρας ἀνασχόμενοι is the aorist middle participle of ἀνέχω, ‘lifting up their hands’, here a gesture of helpless laughter. ἔκθανον ‘died’ is a hyperbole, and γέλῳ is a dative of cause, ‘with laughter’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ὀδυσσεὺς
ἕλκε διὲκ προθύροιο λαβὼν ποδός, ὄφρ’ ἵκετ’ αὐλήν,
αἰθούσης τε θύρας·
sentences.i: Odysseus took him by the foot and dragged him out through the forecourt until he reached the courtyard and the doors of the portico;
sentences.n: ἕλκε is the imperfect, ‘was dragging’. διέκ is ‘right through’, and προθύροιο is the genitive in -οιο of πρόθυρον ‘forecourt’. λαβὼν ποδός ‘taking by the foot’ has the genitive of the part grasped. ὄφρ’ ἵκετ’ is ‘until he came to’, with ἵκετο and its vowel dropped. αὐλήν is the courtyard and θύρας ‘the doors’, both accusatives of the place reached, with αἰθούσης ‘of the portico’ in the genitive. Irus’s threat at 10, ποδὸς ἕλκῃ ‘be dragged by the foot’, is the thing that now happens to him.

sentences.t:
καί μιν ποτὶ ἑρκίον αὐλῆς
εἷσεν ἀνακλίνας·
sentences.l:
and him against the wall of the courtyard
he seated, leaning him back;
sentences.i: and sat him down propped against the courtyard wall;
sentences.n: ποτί is the epic form of πρός ‘against’. ἑρκίον ‘fence, wall’ is formed from ἕρκος ‘fence, enclosure’. εἷσεν is the aorist of ἵζω in the causative sense ‘seated (someone)’, and ἀνακλίνας is ‘leaning (him) back’.

sentences.t:
σκῆπτρον δέ οἱ ἔμβαλε χειρί,
καί μιν φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
and a staff into his hand he thrust,
and, lifting his voice, to him winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: and put a staff in his hand, and lifting his voice he spoke winged words to him:
sentences.n: σκῆπτρον is the beggar’s ‘staff’, the same word that also means ‘sceptre’. οἱ ‘to him’ goes with ἔμβαλε ‘threw in, put into’, and χειρί ‘into his hand’ is a dative of place. φωνήσας is ‘having raised his voice’, and ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα is the stock phrase ‘spoke winged words’.

sentences.t:
ἐνταυθοῖ νῦν ἧσο σύας τε κύνας τ’ ἀπερύκων,
μηδὲ σύ γε ξείνων καὶ πτωχῶν κοίρανος εἶναι
λυγρὸς ἐών, μή πού τι κακὸν καὶ μεῖζον ἐπαύρῃ.
sentences.l:
“Here now sit, keeping off swine and dogs,
and do not you, for your part, of strangers and beggars be ruler,
grievous as you are, lest somehow some evil even greater you get.”
sentences.i: “Sit here now and keep the swine and dogs away, and do not you, grievous as you are, be ruler over strangers and beggars, or you may come by some evil even greater.”
sentences.n: ἐνταυθοῖ is ‘here, to this place’, and ἧσο is the imperative of ἧμαι ‘sit’. ἀπερύκων ‘keeping off’ gives him the work of guarding the door against animals. μηδὲ … εἶναι is an infinitive used as a command, ‘do not be’; κοίρανος is ‘ruler, master’, a bitter word for one who has just tried to order a stranger off the threshold. λυγρὸς ἐών is ‘being grievous’, ἐών being ὤν; λυγρός keeps its one rendering ‘grievous’, though that is hard English of a man. μή πού τι … ἐπαύρῃ is a clause of fear, ‘lest you somehow get’, with ἐπαύρῃ an aorist subjunctive middle of ἐπαυρίσκω ‘get a share of’.
